scenes.text: Teams that build medical devices, cars and medicines must prove, before every release, that each requirement was tested and each safety risk is controlled. Today that proof is a spreadsheet someone rebuilds by hand, and the gaps are found too late. Sometimes by the auditor.

TraceGuard is a Forge app with a Rovo agent. It reads the links your team already keeps in Jira, and turns them into a live traceability matrix, a go or no-go verdict, and an audit report in Confluence. Here is a demo project: the software for an insulin pump, with eight requirements, eight tests and five risks.

I just ask the TraceGuard agent in Rovo chat: is version two point one ready to release? The answer is clear. No-go. Only four of eight requirements are verified, and three high-severity risks are open. It names every gap with its Jira key, and gives the next step. For example, the Bluetooth spoofing risk has no requirement controlling it, and the occlusion alarm test failed.

The same check lives inside the project, as a page. A red verdict at the top. The key numbers: fifty percent coverage, one failed test, three high risks open. And the full matrix: every requirement, the tests that verify it, the risks it controls, and in plain words, why it is not verified. Below, risk control coverage: every hazard, its severity, and what controls it. Every key is a link back to the Jira issue.
One click publishes the evidence to Confluence. The verdict, the matrix and the risk table, dated and linked, ready for an auditor or a design review. No spreadsheet, no copy and paste.

Now the team does its work. The occlusion test is re-run and passes. The missing low-battery test is written. The changed PIN-lock requirement is re-tested. And the spoofing risk is linked to the pairing-confirmation requirement. Refresh, and the release turns green. Go. One hundred percent, no open risks.

TraceGuard is built entirely on Forge, and runs on Atlassian. A Rovo agent with four actions, a UI Kit project page, and Jira and Confluence calls made as the signed-in user, so it only sees what that person is allowed to see. No custom fields and no setup. Just labels and ordinary issue links, that any Jira site already has.

For regulated teams, a missed gap can mean a recall, or a patient at risk. TraceGuard finds those gaps the moment they appear, and turns release day from a scramble into a single question. TraceGuard is decision support. The quality team still owns the decision. Thank you for watching.
